Air mismatch: CIN throw by design into a TB secondary giving up 259 pass yds/game. Ja'Marr Chase is the focal point of the attack.

The CIN host the TB as favorites of 3.5, with the total set at 50.5 — a market that implies a CIN 27–24 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 33% of its snaps with CIN in front, 42% within one score, and 25% with CIN chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

A modest edge to CIN. They should lead more often than not, tilting them slightly toward the run late, while TB leans a touch more pass-heavy to stay in it — but the effect is gentle; this isn't a script that dramatically reshapes anyone's usage.

The Key Matchups

Tough sledding for Chase Brown — TB are stingy against the run (99 yds/game, well below the ~120 norm); lean under on his rushing line.

Efficiency edge to TB — a 46% success-rate offense against a CIN defense that allows 47% — points should come.

Joe Burrow has a passing-yards tailwind — TB allow 259 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Baker Mayfield has a passing-yards tailwind — CIN allow 241 pass yds/game (vs ~230).

Mike Gesicki has room to work — TB allow 40 yds/game to TE1s (vs ~35), a receiving-yards and target angle.

Cade Otton has room to work — CIN allow 46 yds/game to TE1s (vs ~35), a receiving-yards and target angle.

Ja'Marr Chase faces a tough cover — TB hold WR1s to just 52 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Touchdown Board

Mike Gesicki is a live anytime-TD dart — TB are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.43 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

Cade Otton is a live anytime-TD dart — CIN are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.47 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

In the red zone CIN throw it (64% pass inside the 20) — Ja'Marr Chase's TD equity over a goal-line back.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

A modest lean to CIN — they should lead more often than not, nudging them toward the run late and giving Chase Brown a gentle game-script tailwind.

Shootout profile — a 50 total between two non-run-first offenses points to volume passing on both sides; lean into the overs for the pass-catchers.

CIN — a pass-heavy offense

CIN stay aggressive through the air even with a lead — they pass 49% on early downs when ahead versus the league's 44%. They don't sit on the ball, which keeps their receivers live in scripts where most offenses would be running out the clock.

Chase Brown (13 carries, 57 yards projected) gets a mild game-script tailwind as a favorite, though CIN's willingness to keep throwing when ahead caps how much the lead converts into extra carries.

Ja'Marr Chase projects for 9 targets and 84 yards, in line with his established role in a script that neither inflates nor suppresses the pass.

TB — a balanced offense

TB are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (42% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Game script works against the run here — TB project to trail and throw, which squeezes Bucky Irving's rushing projection (15 carries, 66 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Chris Godwin Jr. is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, TB funnel work to their top receiver — 5 targets for 40 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, Cade Otton (TE, 5 targets, 34 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 4-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
